quote: For thou hast brought me with thy question into that same darkness, and into that same cloud of unknowing, that I would thou wert in thyself. For of all other creatures and their works, yea, and of the works of God's self, may a man through grace have fullhead of knowing, and well he can think of them: but of God Himself can no man think. And therefore I would leave all that thing that I can think, and choose to my love that thing that I cannot think. For why; He may well be loved, but not thought. By love may He be gotten and holden; but by thought never. And therefore, although it be good sometime to think of the kindness and the worthiness of God in special, and although it be a light and a part of contemplation: nevertheless yet in this work it shall be cast down and covered with a cloud of forgetting. And thou shalt step above it stalwartly, but listily, with a devout and a pleasing stirring of love, and try for to pierce that darkness above thee. And smite upon that thick cloud of unknowing with a sharp dart of longing love; and go not thence for thing that befalleth.
author: Anonymous
work: The Cloud of Unknowing, chapter 6, ed. Evelyn Underhill (1922)
expansion: The student asks how to think on God, and what God is. The author answers that the question has put him in the same cloud he wishes for the student. Creatures, their works, even the works of God, can be known and thought, by grace, to the full. God himself can be thought by no one. So the teacher would leave everything he can think, and choose for his love the thing he cannot think. The sentence that follows is the book's center: he may well be loved, and not thought; by love he may be gotten and held, and by thought never. Even the consideration of God's kindness, which is a light and a part of contemplation, is, in this particular work, to be put under the cloud of forgetting. One steps above it stalwartly and listily, with a devout stirring of love, and strikes the cloud with a sharp dart of longing, and does not leave for anything that happens.

'Listily' is the author's adverb, from list, longing. The step above holy thoughts is made with desire, with strength. The chapter is the pastoral consequence of the two powers in chapter 4. Because God is incomprehensible to the knowledgeable power, the question 'what is he?' is a question the work cannot answer and should stop entertaining. Because he is comprehensible to love, the dart is the whole method. The author is careful about rank. Thinking of God's goodness is good, and is a part of contemplation. It is simply the wrong part for this work. That distinction saves the book from anti-intellectualism. Theology, meditation on the Passion, reflection on the divine attributes all have their place. They are the lights one agrees to step over when the work of unknowing begins. Underhill's text keeps the vernacular force of 'gotten and holden.' God is not concluded. He is held.

The dart of longing is the book's answer to the charge that negative theology is a refined emptiness. The cloud is thick, and one strikes it. The striking is love with an aim and without an image, and the instruction not to leave 'for thing that befalleth' is a rule of perseverance: consolations, desolations, and interruptions do not adjourn the work. For someone who has grown tired of religious argument and is still drawn to silence, this chapter is the operational core of the English mystical tradition. It is also a critique of the demand, now general, that everything worth loving be something one can think, define, and display. The highest object in the book is defined by the impossibility of that demand, and by the sufficiency of love.

The adverb is a textual argument. Underhill's 1922 text, and the manuscripts she follows, read 'listily,' from list, longing. The step above holy thoughts is made with desire. A widespread reprint, sacred-texts among others, reads 'Mistily,' which turns a word for love's aim into a word for blurred sight. The quote follows the 1922 reading because the method of the chapter depends on it. The dart is sharp. One strikes. The cloud is thick, and the instruction not to leave for anything that happens is a rule of perseverance through consolation and desolation alike. Thinking of God's kindness is granted to be good, and to be a part of contemplation, and to be the wrong part for this work. That ranking is what saves the book from a pose of anti-intellectualism.

John of the Cross, later and in another language, builds a systematic theology of the dark night that this chapter does not attempt. The Cloud is earlier, vernacular, and rude, and it is the English source rather than the Spanish one. Merton's contemplative books return to its center, that God is held by love and is not reached by thought, and they spend a life working out what the holding costs inside a monastery and then, later, outside one. The contemporary pressure the chapter still answers is the demand that whatever is worth loving be something one can define and display. The highest object in the book is specified by the failure of that demand, and by the sufficiency of a longing that has put its images down.

quote: Almost everyone declares that the symmetry of parts towards each other and towards a whole, with, besides, a certain charm of colour, constitutes the beauty recognised by the eye, that in visible things, as indeed in all else, universally, the beautiful thing is essentially symmetrical, patterned. But think what this means. Only a compound can be beautiful, never anything devoid of parts; and only a whole; the several parts will have beauty, not in themselves, but only as working together to give a comely total. Yet beauty in an aggregate demands beauty in details; it cannot be constructed out of ugliness; its law must run throughout. All the loveliness of colour and even the light of the sun, being devoid of parts and so not beautiful by symmetry, must be ruled out of the realm of beauty. And how comes gold to be a beautiful thing? And lightning by night, and the stars, why are these so fair? In sounds also the simple must be proscribed, though often in a whole noble composition each several tone is delicious in itself. Again since the one face, constant in symmetry, appears sometimes fair and sometimes not, can we doubt that beauty is something more than symmetry, that symmetry itself owes its beauty to a remoter principle?
author: Plotinus
work: Ennead I.6, On Beauty, trans. Stephen MacKenna (1917)
expansion: Plotinus states the opinion everyone holds and then dismantles it. Beauty, on that opinion, is symmetry of parts with each other and with the whole, plus a grace of color. He draws the consequence. Only a compound can be beautiful. A simple cannot. The parts of a beautiful whole are beautiful only as contributors, and yet a beautiful whole cannot be built out of ugly parts, so beauty has to run all the way down, which the definition cannot explain. Color and the light of the sun, having no parts, fall out of beauty altogether. So do gold, lightning, the stars. So does a single tone, loved in itself inside a composition whose beauty was supposed to be only the pattern. Last, a face keeps one symmetry and is sometimes fair and sometimes not. Symmetry owes its beauty to a remoter principle. The definition has failed on simples, on the same object at different moments, and, as the argument goes on to say, on virtue and on intellect, where there is nothing to measure.

The opinion he is wrecking is the Stoic and Hellenistic account of beauty as proportion, the account that will keep returning whenever beauty is reduced to a ratio. Plotinus's remoter principle is form, the presence of the intelligible in the sensible, which the rest of I.6 will describe as the soul recognizing its kin. This is why he, and not the theorists of proportion, becomes the source for a metaphysics of light: claritas in Aquinas's three marks of beauty, the sunlike eye in Goethe, the radiance that Romantic and symbolist aesthetics keep trying to name. Proportion is kept, and it is demoted to an instrument. A face can be evenly made and dead. A single color can be alive. MacKenna's 1917 English, from the first volume of his Enneads, has the slow forensic pace of the Greek. The passage is a cross-examination.

The cross-examination still works on every attempt to define beauty as balance, branding, or a measurable harmony of parts. Those accounts go silent in front of a patch of gold, a tone, a face whose proportions have not changed and whose beauty has. Plotinus's remoter principle is the opening through which beauty remains a metaphysical event. The passage shows that it is an arrival from elsewhere, and that the elsewhere is already implied by the things the symmetry theory has to rule out.

The definition he wrecks is the one that keeps returning whenever beauty is handed to a science of proportion. Stoic summetria, Vitruvius, the Renaissance canon of the body, the recurring faith in a golden section: each of them is the opinion the chapter states first and then breaks on simples. A patch of color, a single tone, gold, lightning, a face whose symmetry has not changed and whose beauty has, are the counter-examples. Aquinas receives the Platonic tradition with a triad, integrity, proportion, and claritas. Proportion is kept. Claritas, radiance, is the name of the remoter principle Plotinus is driving toward, the presence of form, which the rest of I.6 will describe as the soul recognizing its kin. Goethe's color and the sunlike eye live on that side of the triad, the side a ratio cannot capture.

Roger Scruton's defense of beauty, much later, as an address from a particular thing that asks to be contemplated for its own sake, is an aesthetic of claritas argued against both a subjectivism of preference and a functionalism of use. He does not need Plotinus's hypostases to inherit Plotinus's objection. If beauty were symmetry, it would be an engineering specification. The passage shows an arrival, and it shows that the things a symmetry theory has to rule out are already evidence for the arrival. That is the opening through which beauty remains a metaphysical event in this whole tradition, from the Enneads to the Romantic symbol and beyond it.

quote: And Nature, asked why it brings forth its works, might answer if it cared to listen and to speak:— "It would have been more becoming to put no question but to learn in silence just as I myself am silent and make no habit of talking. And what is your lesson? This; that whatsoever comes into being is my vision, seen in my silence, the vision that belongs to my character who, sprung from vision, am vision-loving and create vision by the vision-seeing faculty within me. The mathematicians from their vision draw their figures: but I draw nothing: I gaze and the figures of the material world take being as if they fell from my contemplation. As with my Mother (the All-Soul) and the Beings that begot me so it is with me: they are born of a Contemplation and my birth is from them, not by their Act but by their Being; they are the loftier Reason-Principles, they contemplate themselves and I am born."
author: Plotinus
work: Ennead III.8, On Nature, Contemplation, and the One, trans. Stephen MacKenna (1921)
expansion: Plotinus lets Nature speak, and the speech is a rebuke to the question. It would have been better to learn in silence, as Nature herself is silent and does not make a habit of talking. What comes into being is her vision, seen in that silence. She is sprung from vision, loves vision, and creates vision by the seeing power in her. Mathematicians look and then draw. She draws nothing. She gazes, and the figures of the material world take being as if they fell from the gaze. Her mother, the All-Soul, and the beings who begot her, gave her birth in the same way: by being, by contemplation, and not by an act added to their being. They contemplate themselves, and she is born. Production is the overflow of a seeing that does not deliberate.

The tractate's thesis, that everything is striving after contemplation, here reaches the bottom of the sensible world. Nature, which philosophers had treated as a blind maker or as a set of mechanisms, is a weak and silent intellect. The hierarchy of Plotinus's cosmos is a hierarchy of the intensity of seeing: the One, intellect, soul, nature, and then the bodies that fall from nature's gaze. Making is a degraded contemplating, and contemplating is the original making. Schelling's philosophy of nature, in which productivity and the ideal are one act, is the nineteenth-century restatement. Goethe's demand that theory and beholding coincide, and his sense that nature is already at work as a kind of inwardness, belong to the same family, whether or not he is citing III.8. The speech is also a theology of silence. Nature's refusal to talk is the cosmological version of the mystic's refusal to conceptualize. The world is what a silence sees.

The passage turns the prestige of production upside down from the inside. Nature is the great producer, and she produces by not devising. A civilization that understands making only as planning, output, and design has forgotten the mode of making that Plotinus thought was the original one. The relevance for a love of the natural world is direct. A landscape is not a result. It is a gaze that has become visible, and the right answer to it, Nature says, is to learn in silence rather than to demand an account. Contemplation is restored as the high form of creativity, which is the point at which Plotinus, the Romantics, and the contemplative tradition are secretly one tradition.

Schelling's philosophy of nature is the nineteenth-century restatement, and the path of reading is indirect. The Renaissance Neoplatonists and, in his own time, the new editions and discussions around Creuzer made Plotinus available as a philosophy of production rather than only as a piety. In the Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature and in the System of Transcendental Idealism, productivity and the ideal are one act seen from two sides. Nature is visible spirit. Goethe, suspicious of Schelling's system and allied with him against a merely mechanical nature, works the cousin claim on plants and on colors: beholding and theory are to coincide, and metamorphosis is a contemplation one can watch. Steiner, editing that Goethe and wanting a science of the spirit, turns Nature's speech into a discipline with exercises. The silence in which she says she creates becomes a curriculum of perception.

Barfield inherits Steiner's curriculum and Coleridge's imagination together, and the value of his work is the attempt to keep the insight without surrendering criticism. The speech in III.8 remains the original of the family. Making is a degraded and an overflowed contemplating. A civilization that understands production only as planning has forgotten the mode of making the tractate thinks is the first one. A landscape, on this account, is a gaze that has become visible. The instructed response is the one Nature gives the questioner: learn in silence. Contemplation is restored as the high form of creativity, which is where Plotinus, the Romantics, and the contemplative tradition are one tradition.

quote: In the same way, human beings, when weak on the side of contemplation, find in action their trace of vision and of reason: their spiritual feebleness unfits them for contemplation; they are left with a void, because they cannot adequately seize the vision; yet they long for it; they are hurried into action as their way to the vision which they cannot attain by intellection. They act from the desire of seeing their action, and of making it visible and sensible to others when the result shall prove fairly well equal to the plan. Everywhere, doing and making will be found to be either an attenuation or a complement of vision—attenuation if the doer was aiming only at the thing done; complement if he is to possess something nobler to gaze upon than the mere work produced.
author: Plotinus
work: Ennead III.8, On Nature, Contemplation, and the One, trans. Stephen MacKenna (1921)
expansion: The human case follows from Nature's. People who are weak on the side of contemplation still want vision, and they go looking for a trace of it in action. Unable to seize the vision inwardly, they are hurried into doing, so that the deed can be seen by themselves and shown to others, if it turns out reasonably like the plan. Doing and making, Plotinus concludes, are either an attenuation of vision or a complement of it. Attenuation, when the doer wanted only the thing done. Complement, when the doing exists so that there will be something nobler to look at than the work itself. Action is diagnosed as a desire to see, taking the long way because the short way is too hard.

Aristotle, in the last book of the Ethics, had already ranked the contemplative life above the political and practical lives, and called it the activity most like the gods'. He left moral action standing as a genuine human good for composite, embodied beings. Plotinus is harsher and more metaphysical. Action is what contemplation does when it fails to be itself. The complement clause saves him from mere contempt: a deed can be justified if it gives the soul a higher object of vision than the deed. The attenuation clause is the critique. Most busyness wants the product, and the product is a thinned vision. The passage is the ancient source of a suspicion the Romantics, Schopenhauer, and the contemplative writers share, that a life of projects is often a life that could not bear to look. Pieper's defense of leisure as the basis of culture is the twentieth-century restatement in Thomist language: the highest acts are useless in the way vision is useless.

Read now, the passage describes the economy of visibility. People act in order to see the action and to have it seen, and the plan is judged by whether the result can be shown. Plotinus would call that the trace left by a vision one was not strong enough to hold. The practical question he leaves is the complement: can the doing be ordered toward something nobler to gaze on than the work produced? Where it can, action is saved. Where it cannot, action is the shape weakness takes. For a reader tired of production as a moral identity, III.8 is the oldest and still the most exact account of why the tiredness is philosophical.

Aristotle, in the last book of the Ethics, ranks the contemplative life above the political and still defends the practical life as the good of a composite creature who is not a god. Plotinus is harsher. Action is what contemplation does when it cannot seize the vision, or it is a complement, justified when the deed gives the soul something nobler to look at than the deed. The contemplative tradition in the West, the Cloud and Eckhart among them, takes the harsh clause. Josef Pieper's Leisure the Basis of Culture, in 1948, is the Thomist mutation back toward Aristotle, stated against a society that has made total work the meaning of a life. Leisure is the condition of the acts that are useless in the way vision is useless.

Crawford's defense of skilled manual work is a further mutation, and it takes the complement clause as a program. A making in which the material pushes back can be a way of seeing, and the self is situated by the resistance. That is not Plotinus's preference. It is a modern attempt to find the contemplative dignity inside the work, so that action is saved from being only the trace of a vision one was too weak to hold. Read against the economy of visibility, in which people act in order to have the action seen, the passage is still the exact diagnosis. Where the doing is ordered toward something nobler to gaze on than the product, action is a complement. Where it is not, action is the shape the weakness takes.

quote: Every thing which is united is different from the one itself. For if it is united, it will participate in a certain respect of the one, so far as it is said to be united. That, however, which participates of the one, is both one and not one. But the one itself is not both one and not one. For if this were the case, again the one which is in it would have both these, and this would take place to infinity, there being no one itself at which it is possible to stop; but every thing being one and not one, there will be something united which is different from the one. For if the one is the same with the united, it will be infinite multitude. And in a similar manner each of the things of which the united consists will be infinite multitude.
author: Proclus
work: Elements of Theology, proposition IV, trans. Thomas Taylor (1816)
expansion: The proposition is small and the proof is a trap. Everything united is different from the One itself. To be united is to participate the One in some respect, and whatever participates the One is both one and not one. It is one by participation, and not one because participation implies a receiver that is other than the One. The One itself cannot be both one and not one. If it were, the one in it would again be both, and so on without a place to stop. There would be no One itself at which the regress ends. Therefore the united, the composite unity we actually meet, is different from the One. And if one identified them, the One would be an infinite multitude, since every united thing dissolves into further united things. The One is the principle that stops the dissolution. It is not itself a thing that has been unified.

This is henology, the science of the One, as distinct from ontology, the science of being. Plotinus had said that the One is beyond being. Proclus, in the Elements, turns that into a sequence of necessities a student can be examined on. Proposition IV is the moment the composite is forbidden to borrow the name of the principle. Taylor's 1816 English, printed with his translation of the Theology of Plato, is the version in which this logic reached English readers in the Romantic period; Blake's world knew Taylor's Plato, and Taylor's Proclus is the same labor. Dionysius depends on the distinction even where he does not cite it. When the Mystical Theology denies that God is any of the unities we can conceive, it is refusing to let the united stand in for the One. Eckhart's 'one, and above this and that' is the same refusal preached. Later scholarly English, above all Dodds's edition of 1933, is a better critical text. Taylor is the public, complete translation, and his propositions still carry the argument.

The proof is a piece of mental hygiene for anyone who uses the word unity. A unified life, a unified theory, a unified self, a unified culture: each of these is a participation, both one and not one, and none of them is the principle it participates. Confusing them with the One is how systems become idols. Proclus's regress is the formal version of the apophatic rule. Stop at a unity you have assembled, and you are still among composites; the series will ask for a further ground. The relevance to a perennialist instinct, and to the reading of Dionysius, is immediate. The One these writers are pointing at is precisely what cannot appear as a gathered whole. Every whole we can point to has already failed the test of proposition IV.

The proof enters Christian theology by a route that was demonstrated late. In 1895 Hugo Koch and Josef Stiglmayr showed, independently, that the author called Dionysius follows Proclus in detail. The henology of this proposition is therefore inside the Mystical Theology even where the Areopagite does not cite an Elements. Eriugena's Periphyseon carries the distinction of the One from every united thing into the Latin West. Aquinas, commenting on the Divine Names, labors to hold it together with analogy, so that the One beyond being is also the creator who gives the being of creatures. Eckhart's preaching of the One above this and that is less anxious about the guardrail. The united, the composite we can point to, is forbidden at every step to borrow the name of the principle.

Thomas Taylor's English of 1816, printed with his Plato, is the form in which Romantic London could meet the proof. Coleridge's Platonism and the milieu around Blake knew Taylor's labors, whatever particular page they had open. E. R. Dodds's edition of 1933 is a different event: a critical text for classicists, no longer a Romantic scripture, and a better guide to the Greek. Taylor remains the public, complete translation in which the argument did its historical work. The hygiene the proof offers is unchanged. A unified self, a unified theory, a unified culture, is a participation, both one and not one. Treating it as the One is how a composite becomes an idol. The regress is the formal version of the apophatic rule.

quote: For if multitude is prior to the one, the one indeed will participate of multitude, but multitude which is prior to the one will not participate of the one, since that multitude existed prior to the subsistence of the one. For it will not participate of that which is not; because that which participates of the one, is one and at the same time not one; but the one will not yet subsist, that which is first being multitude. It is, however, impossible that there should be a certain multitude, which in no respect whatever participates of the one. Multitude, therefore, is not prior to the one.
author: Proclus
work: Elements of Theology, proposition V, trans. Thomas Taylor (1816)
expansion: Proposition V is the companion proof, run as a reductio. Suppose multitude were prior to the One. Then the One would participate multitude, while multitude, being prior, would not participate the One, since the One would not yet be there to participate. Participation in what is not is nothing. And a multitude that in no respect participates the One is impossible: each of its members would be a multitude, and each of those another, an infinite of infinites, with nothing one anywhere for the division to stop. Therefore multitude is not prior to the One. The One is first because, without a prior unity, many cannot even be many. Manyness is a late condition. It presupposes the principle it seems to threaten.

Together with proposition IV, this is the opening move of the whole Proclean system. Procession, the derivation of lower orders from higher, can begin only once the One is safe from two confusions: from being a composite, and from being secondary to the many. Christian Platonism inherits both safeguards. Dionysius's God is the cause of all multitude and is not a member of it. Creation, in the scholastic development, will restate the priority as the priority of simple being over composed beings, with differences Proclus would not accept, since he does not have a creator in the biblical sense. The logical nerve travels anyway. Taylor's translation makes the nerve available in the English in which Coleridge, and the Platonic undercurrent of Romanticism, could meet it. The proof is also why 'the many' is never, in this tradition, a first principle. Atomism, pluralism, and the prestige of sheer variety are, by this argument, descriptions of something that has already fallen from a unity they depend on.

The reductio is a good instrument against the assumption, now nearly invisible, that plurality is the natural starting point and unity a late, optional achievement, something groups and theories may or may not reach. Proclus says the many cannot be there first. A world of items, data, and positions still owes its countability to a one it does not contain. That is a metaphysical claim, and it is also a contemplative one: attention that stops at the scatter has stopped too soon, because the scatter was never able to found itself. The passage is the driest page in this set, and it is the floor under the others. Eckhart's One above this and that, Dionysius's God beyond every name, Plotinus's source of beauty, all of them require that the principle be prior to the multitude of things it makes beautiful, knowable, and real.

Christian Platonism inherits the priority and changes the verb. Proclus's One does not choose, and it does not make a world from nothing. Creation, as the scholastics develop it, restates the dependence of the many on the One as the free gift of being by a God who is not a member of the series. That is a mutation the Elements will not underwrite, and the logical nerve travels anyway: multitude cannot be there first. Dionysius's God is the cause of all multitude and is not an item in it. The perennialist reading, Guénon's in particular, takes the same priority as evidence that the great traditions agree on a first principle. The agreement, such as it is, begins only after this proof. Everything that distinguishes emanation from creation, and a metaphysical One from the God of Abraham, is a later decision about how the dependence is told. Flattening those decisions is not what proposition V says.

The contemporary assumption the reductio still cuts against is quiet and nearly invisible. Plurality is treated as the natural starting point, and unity as an optional late achievement of groups and of theories. Proclus says the many cannot found themselves. A world of items, data, and positions owes its countability to a one it does not contain. The contemplative form of that claim is the one the rest of this set keeps spending: attention that stops at the scatter has stopped too soon. Eckhart's One above this and that, Dionysius's God beyond every name, and Plotinus's source of beauty all require the principle to be prior to the multitude of things it makes real.

quote: Concrete ideas are formed by us on the basis of our concepts by means of the imagination. Hence what the free spirit needs in order to realise his concepts, in order to assert himself in the world, is moral imagination. This is the source of the free spirit’s action. Only those men, therefore, who are endowed with moral imagination are, properly speaking, morally productive. Those who merely preach morality, i.e., those who merely excogitate moral rules without being able to condense them into concrete ideas, are morally unproductive. They are like those critics who can explain very competently how a work of art ought to be made, but who are themselves incapable of the smallest artistic production.
author: Rudolf Steiner
work: The Philosophy of Spiritual Activity, trans. R. F. Alfred Hoernlé (1922 edition)
expansion: Moral imagination is Steiner's name for the act that makes a free agent. A concept of what ought to be done stays inert until imagination condenses it into a concrete idea, fitted to a perceptible situation. The people he calls morally unproductive are the ones who can say how an action ought to look and cannot produce one. He reaches for the analogy of the critic who knows how a work of art should be made and cannot make the smallest one. Freedom, in this book, is the capacity to determine from oneself the ideas that will underlie action. A mechanical process does not do it, and a God standing outside the agent does not do it either.

The book is the early Steiner, the Philosophy of Freedom of 1894, in the Hoernlé English of 1916 as revised for the 1922 edition. It is a philosophy of ethical individualism written before anthroposophy became a movement with exercises and a cosmology. He is arguing with Kant. The categorical imperative, a law that arrives as a command from beyond the agent's own insight, is exactly what moral imagination is there to replace. He is also arguing with a crude evolutionary ethics that would measure a new moral idea by an old species and call the new one degenerate. A new moral idea is no more illegitimate, on his monism, than a new organic form.

Goethe is the method behind the argument even where this chapter is talking about conduct. Steiner had edited Goethe's scientific writings and taken metamorphosis as the pattern of a thinking that stays with the phenomenon and lets a form transform. Moral imagination is metamorphosis in the practical sphere: a principle becomes an individual deed without being copied from a template. Barfield will later treat this, together with Coleridge, as the seed of a conscious participation. The danger, which Steiner himself notes against immature readers, is that an undeveloped impulse announces itself as a moral intuition. The theory is about a mature spirit's concrete idea, and it is an account of freedom as productivity.

quote: It is not the task of knowledge to reproduce in conceptual form something already existing independently. Its task is to create a wholly new realm which, united with the world of sense-data, ends by yielding us reality in the full sense. In this way, man’s supreme activity, the creative productivity of his spirit, finds its organic place in the universal world-process. Without this activity it would be impossible to conceive the world-process as a totality complete in itself. Man does not confront the world-process as a passive spectator who merely copies in his mind the events which occur, without his participation, in the cosmos without. He is an active co-creator in the world-process, and his knowledge is the most perfect member of the organism of the universe. This view carries with it an important consequence for our conduct, for our moral ideals. These, too, must be regarded, not as copies of an external standard, but as rooted within us. Similarly, we refuse to look upon our moral laws as the behests of any power outside us. We know no “categorical imperative” which, like a voice from the Beyond, prescribes to us what to do or to leave undone.
author: Rudolf Steiner
work: The Philosophy of Spiritual Activity, appendix on Truth and Science, trans. R. F. Alfred Hoernlé (1922 edition)
expansion: The appendix states the epistemology the ethics depends on. Knowing is not the copying of a world that is already finished without the knower. Thinking produces a content of its own, and only when that content is united with what the senses give is there reality in the full sense. The human being is therefore a co-creator in the world-process, and knowledge is, in his phrase, the most perfect member of the organism of the universe. Hoernlé's English says the events occur 'in the cosmos without,' meaning the cosmos outside the spectator. The stiffness is the translator's. The claim is that the spectator-picture of knowledge is already a false moral picture, because it makes the agent someone who receives ends from elsewhere.

From the epistemology he draws the consequence for ideals. They are rooted in the agent. There is no voice from the Beyond prescribing what to do or to leave undone. He names Kant's categorical imperative in order to refuse it. Moral ideals are free creations. This is the same refusal the chapter on moral imagination makes from the side of action, here made from the side of truth. A truth that is only a copy cannot found a freedom. A truth that is an act can.

The mutation into later Steiner, and then into Barfield, is the mutation of a critical point into a story about consciousness. Here the co-creation is the ordinary, if usually unnoticed, work of thinking joining percepts. In the anthroposophical writings the same conviction becomes a path of higher knowledge, with definite exercises. Barfield's final participation is the historical form: a culture that has withdrawn from participation in its representations could come to participate again, knowingly, without returning to an archaic fusion. Goethe's irony, the demand to theorise while knowing that one is theorising, is the safeguard this appendix does not yet emphasize. Co-creation without that irony becomes the fantasy that the spirit posits the world. Held with the irony, it is the claim that a world described as if no one were thinking it has not been fully described.

quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances. And as the past grows without ceasing, so also there is no limit to its preservation. Memory, as we have tried to prove, is not a faculty of putting away recollections in a drawer, or of inscribing them in a register. There is no register, no drawer; there is not even, properly speaking, a faculty, for a faculty works intermittently, when it will or when it can, whilst the piling up of the past upon the past goes on without relaxation. In reality, the past is preserved by itself, automatically. In its entirety, probably, it follows us at every instant; all that we have felt, thought and willed from our earliest infancy is there, leaning over the present which is about to join it, pressing against the portals of consciousness that would fain leave it outside.
author: Henri Bergson
work: Creative Evolution, chapter 1, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911)
expansion: Duration, in the opening of Creative Evolution, is the past gnawing into the future and swelling as it advances. Memory is not a faculty that files recollections in a drawer. The past preserves itself. In its entirety it leans on the present, and the brain's work, as he will say in the next sentences, is mostly to hold it back so that action can go forward. What matters in the sentences here is the refusal of a psychology of states. If inner life were solid beads on a solid thread, there would be no duration. The beads are what attention and language make when they need something logic can handle. Under the symbols, time is the stuff of psychical life.

The book of 1907 applies to life a result he had argued in 1889, in Time and Free Will: real duration is undivided continuity and creation, and it is falsified as soon as it is spread out in space. Mitchell's 1911 English is the translation in which this reached American and British readers, William James among the sympathetic. The mutation from the early essay to Creative Evolution is the mutation from a psychology of consciousness to a metaphysics of the living world. The past that presses on the present becomes the pattern of an élan, a vital impetus, which he will oppose both to a mechanism in which everything is given and to a finalism in which the end is given.

The page still cuts against a picture of the self as a sequence of replaceable states, a profile, a dataset, a present with no weight. Character, he says in the sentences that follow these, is the condensation of a history, and we desire with the whole of it even when we think with a small part. That is why a moment cannot be repeated. The circumstances might return. The person they would meet has already been changed by having lived them. Irreversibility is the moral fact inside the metaphysics. A culture of resets and of optimized presents is a culture that has chosen the drawer.

quote: This is what the cinematograph does. With photographs, each of which represents the regiment in a fixed attitude, it reconstitutes the mobility of the regiment marching. It is true that if we had to do with photographs alone, however much we might look at them, we should never see them animated: with immobility set beside immobility, even endlessly, we could never make movement. In order that the pictures may be animated, there must be movement somewhere. The movement does indeed exist here; it is in the apparatus. It is because the film of the cinematograph unrolls, bringing in turn the different photographs of the scene to continue each other, that each actor of the scene recovers his mobility; he strings all his successive attitudes on the invisible movement of the film. The process then consists in extracting from all the movements peculiar to all the figures an impersonal movement abstract and simple, movement in general, so to speak: we put this into the apparatus, and we reconstitute the individuality of each particular movement by combining this nameless movement with the per sonal attitudes. Such is the contrivance of the cinematograph. And such is also that of our knowledge. Instead of attaching ourselves to the inner becoming of things, we place ourselves outside them in order to recompose their becoming artificially.
author: Henri Bergson
work: Creative Evolution, chapter 4, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911)
expansion: The cinematograph is his model of the intellect at work on becoming. Snapshots of a marching regiment, each one a fixed attitude, are thrown in rapid succession, and the mobility seems to return. It returns only because there is movement in the apparatus, the unrolling of the film. From the particular movements one has extracted an impersonal movement-in-general, put it in the machine, and recombined it with the attitudes. Knowledge, he says, does the same. It places itself outside the inner becoming of things and recomposes that becoming artificially. Perception, intellection, and language are this contrivance. Ordinary knowledge is cinematographical.

The polemic is aimed at a way of thinking he traces from Zeno's paradoxes to the Platonic idea and on into modern science. The idea, eidos, is a stable view taken of an instability, a snapshot that has had its thread to time cut and has then been treated as more real than the change. He is not dismissing Plato's whole ambition. He is saying that a metaphysics built by the cinematographical habit will always set eternity above time, and will always be surprised that the snapshots, set beside one another, never quite yield the movement. The practical success of the habit is not in dispute. Action needs stops. Speculation that uses only stops misses what life is doing.

Proust, who was related to Bergson by marriage and who built a novel on involuntary memory, is the literary mutation: the past returns as a whole, not as a fact retrieved from storage, which is what the first chapter's account of duration had described. Deleuze's Bergsonism, much later, makes the virtual and the actual into a philosophy of cinema itself, a reversal in which the apparatus Bergson used as a figure of illusion becomes an art that can think time. The figure's original force is the simpler one. A sequence of states is not a life. The movement is in the apparatus, or it is nowhere. Attention that wants the real has to get inside the transition the snapshots were taken to avoid.

quote: Yet if the only form of tradition, of handing down, consisted in following the ways of the immediate generation before us in a blind or timid adherence to its successes, “tradition” should positively be discouraged. We have seen many such simple currents soon lost in the sand; and novelty is better than repetition. Tradition is a matter of much wider significance. It cannot be inherited, and if you want it you must obtain it by great labour. It involves, in the first place, the historical sense, which we may call nearly indispensable to anyone who would continue to be a poet beyond his twenty-fifth year; and the historical sense involves a perception, not only of the pastness of the past, but of its presence; the historical sense compels a man to write not merely with his own generation in his bones, but with a feeling that the whole of the literature of Europe from Homer and within it the whole of the literature of his own country has a simultaneous existence and composes a simultaneous order. This historical sense, which is a sense of the timeless as well as of the temporal and of the timeless and of the temporal together, is what makes a writer traditional. And it is at the same time what makes a writer most acutely conscious of his place in time, of his contemporaneity.
author: T. S. Eliot
work: The Sacred Wood, 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1920)
expansion: Tradition, in the essay of 1919 collected the next year, is a labor, not an inheritance. Following the previous generation is the form of it he thinks should be discouraged. Novelty is better than that kind of repetition. What he requires instead is the historical sense: the pastness of the past and the presence of the past, felt together, so that the literature of Europe from Homer, and the literature of one's own country inside it, exists simultaneously and composes an order. That sense is what makes a writer traditional, and it is what makes him know his own contemporaneity. The timeless and the temporal are not alternatives. The sense of them together is the qualification.

The essay belongs to the early Eliot, the critic of The Sacred Wood, before the conversion of 1927 and before Four Quartets. Its immediate enemies are a Romantic cult of the poet's difference and a Georgian comfort with the previous generation's successes. The individuality worth having, he has just argued, is often the place where the dead poets assert themselves most vigorously. The historical sense is the condition for that individuality. It is also the seed of the later poems' concern with time. What the essay states as a principle of criticism, the poems will try to live as a pattern of moments in which a life is answerable to more than its succession.

The responsibility he names is easy to sentimentalize into a respect for the canon. Read strictly, it is harder. The existing order is complete before the new work arrives, and for order to persist the whole order has to be, however slightly, altered. The past is changed by the present. Conformity of the kind that leaves both untouched is not conformity. A writer who wants the tradition as a shelter from the present has missed the essay. A writer who wants the present as a liberation from the dead has missed it too. The labor is the labor of holding both, which is the labor Four Quartets will not let him set down.

quote: Blake was endowed with a capacity for considerable understanding of human nature, with a remarkable and original sense of language and the music of language, and a gift of hallucinated vision. Had these been controlled by a respect for impersonal reason, for common sense, for the objectivity of science, it would have been better for him. What his genius required, and what it sadly lacked, was a framework of accepted and traditional ideas which would have prevented him from indulging in a philosophy of his own, and concentrated his attention upon the problems of the poet. Confusion of thought, emotion, and vision is what we find in such a work as _Also Sprach Zarathustra_; it is eminently not a Latin virtue. The concentration resulting from a framework of mythology and theology and philosophy is one of the reasons why Dante is a classic, and Blake only a poet of genius. The fault is perhaps not with Blake himself, but with the environment which failed to provide what such a poet needed; perhaps the circumstances compelled him to fabricate, perhaps the poet required the philosopher and mythologist; although the conscious Blake may have been quite unconscious of the motives.
author: T. S. Eliot
work: The Sacred Wood, 'Blake' (1920)
expansion: The essay praises Blake's eye and then refuses his system. A remarkable sense of language, a gift of hallucinated vision, and a real understanding of human nature were, Eliot thinks, left without the framework that would have concentrated them. Impersonal reason, common sense, the objectivity of science, a mythology and a theology already accepted: these would have kept Blake on the problems of the poet. Instead, Eliot says, England handed him an empty place where a continuous religious history might have been, and he fabricated a philosophy out of odds and ends, ingenious in the way homemade furniture is ingenious. Dante is a classic because of the concentration a traditional framework gives. Blake remains a poet of genius. The fault is charged as much to the environment as to the man.

The judgment is 1920, and it is a young classicist's judgment. It sits beside 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' as the case study. Blake is what a great gift does when the historical sense has no order to join. Eliot's example of the confusion of thought, emotion, and vision is Nietzsche's Zarathustra, which tells you which kind of homemade metaphysics he is unwilling to admire. The Latinity he wants is Dante's, a philosophy inside the poem because it was the philosophy of a world, not a philosophy the poet had to invent in order to have a world.

Kathleen Raine's life's work is the argued reply. In Blake and Tradition and in Defending Ancient Springs she holds that Blake's mythology is learned, a reception of Plato, Plotinus, Boehme, and the Hermetic writings, and that what Eliot called odds and ends is a tradition he had not recognized. The mutation is a lesson in how a criticism creates the scholarship that overturns it. Eliot's demand for a framework remains serious. Raine's claim is that Blake had one, and that the English suspicion of visionary poetry as crankiness is a failure to read the framework. Between them is the question this whole set keeps meeting: whether imagination is a private fabrication or an organ that joins a real order.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Barfield treats the history of language as a history of the splitting of meanings. In early speech, what we now separate as the literal and the metaphorical was one concrete figure. The word did not point at a bare object and then, optionally, decorate it. Object and meaning arrived together. Poetic Diction argues that poetry is the place where that lost unity can be remembered and, in flashes, restored. Saving the Appearances extends the claim from words to perception. Original participation is his name for a consciousness in which the world is experienced as meaningful from within, not as a set of objects represented to a subject standing outside them. The scientific revolution, as he reads Galileo, Locke, and the new experimental philosophy, withdraws that participation. What remains are collective representations, appearances produced by a culture, which the culture then takes for things in themselves. He calls that mistake idolatry. Final participation would be a free, conscious recovery of participation, chosen rather than inherited, and it would not be a return to the archaic fusion.
author: Owen Barfield
work: Poetic Diction (1928) and Saving the Appearances (1957); paraphrase, not a quotation

Final participation would be a free, conscious recovery of participation, chosen rather than inherited, and it would not be a return to the archaic fusion.

The reading list behind the claim is specific. Coleridge's distinction of imagination from fancy, and his struggle with a dead world of objects, is the Romantic source. Goethe's way of science, in which the observer and the phenomenon belong to one act, is the second. Steiner's Philosophy of Freedom and the later anthroposophy are the third, and Barfield defended them in public, including in Romanticism Comes of Age, while trying to keep a critical standard Steiner's movement did not always want. The Inklings argued the consequence. Lewis conducted a long correspondence with Barfield, their Great War, resisting what he heard as a slide into subjectivism. Tolkien's sense that language is not a code laid over a finished world carries the mark of Barfield's theory of meaning.

Set beside this set of passages, Barfield is the historian of a change the others describe from inside. Goethe's sunlike eye and his irony about theorising are, in Barfield's terms, exercises of participation that know themselves as exercises. Plotinus's soul recognizing its kin in the beautiful is an ancient form of the same kinship. Charles Taylor will later describe the buffered self and the immanent frame as the felt result of the withdrawal, without Barfield's prescription of a final participation. Jean Gebser's structures of consciousness are a cousin map, drawn independently. The likeness is real. A line of reading from Gebser to Barfield should not be invented.

The present use is a diagnosis of representation. A life conducted on screens, models, and metrics is a life inside idolatry in his exact sense: appearances taken for the things. The remedy he hoped for was not less thinking. It was a thinking that participates again, knowingly. That hope is the modern form of Goethe's demand to theorise with irony, and of Steiner's claim that knowledge is a co-creation. It is also the reason his work belongs with a love of landscape and of poetic speech. Both are, for him, evidence that meaning is not a coating we add to a bare world.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The lecture, given as the Andrew Lang lecture in 1939 and published in 1947 in a volume in honor of Charles Williams, defends the fairy-story as a serious form and refuses the idea that it is native to children. Tolkien distinguishes three faces of the art he calls recovery, escape, and consolation. Recovery is a regaining of sight, so that things long dulled by familiarity are seen again as what they are. Escape he defends as the escape of a prisoner, and he refuses the sneer that calls it desertion. Consolation is the sudden joyous turn he names eucatastrophe, the opposite of the tragic catastrophe, a grace of the story's ending that does not deny the sorrow it answers. Around these he sets sub-creation: the making of a secondary world with the inner consistency of reality. The human maker works with what is already given, and the making is a real making. He then makes the theological wager that the Christian story has the shape of a fairy-story that has entered history, so that the joy the art offers is answered by a truth of the same shape.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
work: On Fairy-Stories (lecture 1939, published 1947); paraphrase, not a quotation
expansion: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The lecture, given as the Andrew Lang lecture in 1939 and published in 1947 in a volume in honor of Charles Williams, defends the fairy-story as a serious form and refuses the idea that it is native to children. Tolkien distinguishes three faces of the art he calls recovery, escape, and consolation. Recovery is a regaining of sight, so that things long dulled by familiarity are seen again as what they are. Escape he defends as the escape of a prisoner, and he refuses the sneer that calls it desertion. Consolation is the sudden joyous turn he names eucatastrophe, the opposite of the tragic catastrophe, a grace of the story's ending that does not deny the sorrow it answers. Around these he sets sub-creation: the making of a secondary world with the inner consistency of reality. The human maker works with what is already given, and the making is a real making. He then makes the theological wager that the Christian story has the shape of a fairy-story that has entered history, so that the joy the art offers is answered by a truth of the same shape.

The lecture is an Inkling argument, addressed to the same room as Williams's doctrine of exchange and Lewis's long defense of myth as a vehicle of truth. Tolkien had reservations about George MacDonald, whose fairy tales he found mixed, and he had none about the dignity of the form. Coleridge's imagination is in the background of sub-creation. Barfield's account of meaning is in the background of the claim that the fantastic is a way of seeing and not a coating on the real. The publication in a book for Williams matters. Eucatastrophe and coinherence are neighboring answers to the question of how a sorrow and a joy can inhabit one story without either cancelling the other.

The mutation from Romantic wonder to this lecture is the addition of history. Novalis can lift the veil inside a dream and find the beloved. Tolkien wants a turn that is still a turn of story and that he is willing to say has happened in the primary world. That is his difference from a symbolism that never risks a fact, and from a realism that never risks a joy. Lewis, moving in the same years from a love of myth toward a claim about fact, is the parallel case, argued in a different temperament.

The lecture is a criticism of a culture that files wonder under childhood and files adulthood under disenchantment. Recovery is a discipline of attention: the trite thing, seen again, is the test. Escape, in his sense, judges a world by whether a reasonable person would want to flee it, and it calls the wish sanity. Consolation refuses the prestige of the unhappy ending. For a reader drawn to myth, to the imaginal, and to a Christianity that does not apologize for joy, the essay is the twentieth-century statement of why those loves are one love.

Lives inhere in one another, and the City of God is the social form of that fact, practiced under the conditions of the fall as exchange and substitution: one person can bear what is properly another's, and the bearing is a real spiritual act, not a metaphor for sympathy. The sources are Dante, the theology of the Body of Christ as a real coinherence of members, and a novelist’s sense of the city of London as already a web of substituted lives. Eliot published him at Faber and wrote on him after his death in 1945. Lewis’s Arthurian poetry and The Four Loves are marked by the doctrine of exchange. Auden read him with an admiration that left traces in the later poems. Williams is the Inkling whose theology is least easily reduced to apologetics, because the claim is metaphysical and practical at once: the way things are is that we are in one another, and the way to live is to bear one another on purpose.

Set against the negative tradition in this set, he is the advocate of the other half. The Cloud’s cloud of forgetting is the rejection of images, and Williams would say it is true and incomplete. Eckhart’s letting-go of God for God’s sake is the extreme of rejection. Beatrice is the extreme of affirmation, a creature through whom glory is seen without the creature being dissolved into a mere sign. The Romantic marriage of Hyacinth and Rosebud is a tale of affirmation. Williams gives that tale a dogmatic name and a practice.

The other keeps the unknowing and loses the world. Williams’s claim is that the two ways are one life, and that substitution is how the life becomes social. A culture of buffered selves, each the proprietor of a private interior, is the practical denial of coinherence. His books are the twentieth-century English argument that the denial is false to the way persons actually exist.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Merton distinguishes a false self from a true one. The false self is the social ego, built of desires, fears, and the roles a life uses to make itself feel real. The true self is hidden in God and is not identical with those roles. Contemplation, as New Seeds of Contemplation describes it, is not a psychological state one produces by technique. It is a gift of unknowing, a simple intuition born of love, closer to the Cloud of Unknowing and to John of the Cross than to a method of mental silence. The early Merton, in The Seven Storey Mountain and the first Seeds of Contemplation, can sound like a flight from the world. The later journals, Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander and the Asian Journal, revise that flight. Contemplation is worked out inside history, in friendship with the world, and in a serious meeting with Zen. The false self remains the problem. The world is no longer the name of it.

He read the English mystics in Underhill’s recovery of them, and he read Eckhart seriously in the 1950s and 1960s, taking the spark, the uncreated ground, as the point where a Christian account of the self and a Zen account of emptiness could speak. That meeting is his own mutation of Eckhart, who did not know Zen. Weil’s attention is a parallel modern discipline, more moral and less monastic. Merton’s version stays inside a vowed life even when the later books open the monastery gates. The lineage behind the false self runs from the Pauline old man through the Desert Fathers’ logismoi, the distracting thoughts, to the Cloud’s warning that a person may love the goods of God in place of God.

A contemplation defined against the world becomes a contemplation that can love the world without confusing the world with the self. That is the twentieth-century form of Williams’s two ways, lived by a monk who began on the way of rejection and had to learn affirmation without abandoning the cell. His journals are the record of the learning.

The false self is now a culture’s ordinary product: a profile, a performance, a stream of positions. Merton’s claim is that this construction is not the person, and that the way past it is not a better performance. Unknowing, in his sense, is the undoing of the construction in the presence of a God who is not one of its materials. The later Merton adds that the undoing does not require a hatred of the city, the body, or the neighbor. That addition is what keeps the doctrine from becoming another costume of the false self, the costume of the person who has risen above the world.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Wound of Knowledge reads the history of Christian spirituality, from the New Testament to John of the Cross, as a knowledge that arrives through the failure of the self’s projects. Spirituality, on this account, is not a technique for rising above suffering and the body. It is what happens to speech about God when a life is brought up against its limits. The negative way belongs inside that history. Apophatic language, the unsaying of names, is bound to the particularity of Christ and to the wounds of time. It is not a free-floating method of emptying the mind, and it is not a refusal of the Incarnation. Williams returns often to the point that the God who exceeds every concept is the God who has spoken in a life, so that negative theology and attention to the concrete are one discipline. The wound is epistemological. One learns by being brought to the end of what one was able to say.

The book is a historian’s book, written by a theologian who would later be Archbishop of Canterbury, and its sources are the ones this set already lives with: the Gospels, Augustine, Dionysius, the desert and medieval traditions, John of the Cross. His difference from a purely philosophical apophasis, Eckhart’s most daring sentences or Dionysius read as a system, is the insistence on the narrative and the body. Unknowing that has detached itself from Israel, from the Passion, and from the neighbor is, for him, another gnosis, a knowledge for a self that would rather not be historical. That criticism is his argument with a certain modern taste for mysticism as an escape from doctrine.

He is also an heir of Weil in a quieter way than Murdoch is. Affliction, the kind of suffering that unmakes a person’s world, is treated as a place of knowledge and not only as a problem for theodicy. Where Weil’s decreation can sound like a metaphysics of the void, Williams keeps the wound inside a story of a God who has already gone into it. The mutation is from an ethic of attention to a Christology of attention.

The use of the book now is the refusal of two shortcuts. One shortcut is a positive theology so sure of its names that it has nothing to learn from silence. The other is a negative theology so pleased with unsaying that it never has to speak of a particular body. Williams’s history says that the tradition’s greatest writers were people whose speech failed them in front of something, and that the failure was the knowledge. For a reader trying to hold Eckhart and the Creed in one life, the book is the twentieth-century map of how that holding has actually been done.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Weil’s central moral notion is attention. It is a negative effort, a waiting in which the greed of the self to seize, to explain, and to console itself is suspended so that a reality can appear. Affliction, malheur, is her name for a suffering that does not only hurt the body but destroys the person, the social and inward world that had made a life feel like a life. Decreation is the undoing of the imaginary self, so that what is created can pass through a human being without being confiscated by the ego. She treats the love of the order of the world and the love of the neighbor in affliction as one love. Plato’s Good beyond being, the Bhagavad Gita’s action without attachment, and the Christian mystics, John of the Cross especially, are the texts she makes speak to one another. The notebooks published after her death in 1943, edited into Gravity and Grace and Waiting for God, are where these notions were given to readers. They are not a system she finished.

Merton recognizes the kinship with contemplation and lives it inside a church she approached and never simply joined. Kingsnorth, Berry, and the critics of the Machine cite her on uprootedness and on attention as what a humane life requires. Each heir drops something. Murdoch drops the mystical metaphysics. The political readers sometimes drop the severity about the self. The notebooks hold both, which is why they remain difficult.

Copyright keeps her sentences out of this file. The ideas are stated here as ideas, and the books are the place where her wording does the work. What this set can say without those sentences is the connection. Her attention is the Cloud’s loving power, translated into an ethic that can stand in a factory and in front of an afflicted neighbor. Decreation is Eckhart’s poverty, translated into a psychology of the imaginary self. The translation is the twentieth century’s, and it is one of the ways the older pages still bite.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Sovereignty of Good, three essays from the years around 1970, argues that the moral life is a life of attention and not a series of acts of will. The enemy is a picture she found both in the existentialism of her time and in the linguistic philosophy around her: a solitary will that chooses, in a naked moment, among values it has not been shaped by. She treats the ego as a greedy persistence. Goodness is its gradual defeat. Beauty is one of the ordinary places the defeat begins, because a beautiful thing draws attention off the self before the self has decided to be good. The Good itself she describes, with Plato, as a magnetic focus, real, not a person, and not a formula. An attentive, loving look at a particular reality, a face, a kestrel, a work of art, is what she means by the virtue of attention, and she says plainly that the notion comes from Simone Weil. Art, especially the realistic novel, matters because it trains that gaze. Fantasy, the ego’s self-soothing story, is the opposite of attention.

Murdoch keeps decreation’s psychology, the undoing of the greedy self, and she is wary of Weil’s more extreme metaphysics of affliction and the void. She wants the world to remain, seen accurately and therefore loved. Unselfing is for the sake of the real, not for the sake of an escape from it.

Schopenhauer’s ethical sublime is a structural ancestor she does not need to claim. Knowledge holding its ground where the will would seize is his description and, in another vocabulary, hers. The difference is the destination. He is on the way to the denial of the will. She is on the way to a Good that justifies the endless effort of seeing. Keats’s claim that Beauty obliterates consideration is a Romantic cousin of her claim that beauty is an occasion of unselfing, with the difference that she trusts a long discipline of attention more than she trusts a poetic annihilation.

The essays are a criticism of a culture that has made sincerity and choice the whole of ethics. If the will is the only moral faculty, then a strong preference, authentically felt, is already a moral achievement. Murdoch thinks that is the ego congratulating itself. The counter-picture is slow, local, and perceptual. One learns to see a particular person who is not a function of one’s need. That is the same labor the ethical sublime described and the same labor Weil called attention, stated for a secular reader who still wants the Good to be more than a preference.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Bachelard’s career turns on a reversal. In the earlier epistemological books, of which The Psychoanalysis of Fire is the imaginative case, the image is an obstacle. Scientific thought has to psychoanalyze itself free of the dreams that cluster around fire, water, and the other elements, because those dreams distort the concepts. In the later books, The Poetics of Space and The Poetics of Reverie above all, the same images are no longer obstacles. Reverie is a primary mode of consciousness. It is not the nocturnal dream, which overwhelms the dreamer. It is a waking, valorizing imagination in which the dreamer is present and the image gives the world a value. He distinguishes a material imagination, which cleaves to the elements, from a formal imagination, which draws outlines. The elements are not metaphors one chooses. They are the materials in which imagination actually works, and each has its own cosmos of images.

The reversal is the thing to watch, because it is a mutation inside one mind. The philosopher of the epistemological break, close to a rationalist severity about what counts as knowledge, becomes the phenomenologist of the poetic image. He does not cancel the early work. He changes the status of what it had called an obstacle. The image is an obstacle for the concept and a truth for the imagination, and both descriptions can stand if one stops demanding that imagination justify itself before the sciences. That settlement is his gift to a Romantic tradition that had always trusted the image and had lacked a patient description of how an image holds a consciousness.

Novalis’s dream-room, Goethe’s insistence that a phenomenon carries its own theory, and Jung’s archetypal image are the neighborhood. Bachelard is cooler than Jung. He does not found a therapy, and he is wary of reducing the image to a hidden complex, which is what his own early ‘psychoanalysis’ of the elements risked. The later poetics lets the image be an origin. Hillman and the archetypal psychologists read him as an ally in the defense of the image against the concept. Corbin would add that a phenomenology of reverie is still a description of a subject, and that the imaginal world is not exhausted by the reverie that perceives it.

The present use is the rehabilitation of a kind of thinking that a technical culture classifies as mood. Reverie, in his late sense, is a way of knowing value. A house, a flame, a drawer, a shell, holds a consciousness and teaches it what intimacy, secrecy, and vastness are. The education of attention that runs through Weil, Murdoch, and the contemplatives has, in Bachelard, its poetic phenomenology. One learns the world by dreaming it well, awake.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Poetics of Space studies the house as a topography of intimacy. Rooms, cellars, attics, drawers, chests, nests, and shells are not illustrations of psychological facts one already has. They are the spaces in which intimacy, secrecy, and refuge are actually imagined, and therefore the spaces in which those experiences take on their form. The miniature, a thing small enough to be dominated by the gaze, and the vast, a thing large enough to overwhelm it, are two poles of the same imagination of space. He calls the method a phenomenology of the image: one receives the image in its suddenness, before the habits of criticism have reduced it to a cause. The house one was born in is, on this account, more than a scene of memory. It is a body of images that continues to organize how a later life feels shelter and exposure.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Giegerich, a Jungian analyst, argues that soul is logical life. It is the inwardness of thought thinking itself, not a place inside the person where images are stored and not a mythic land one visits. He thinks much archetypal psychology, Hillman’s included, still pictures the soul as a realm of figures, and that this picture literalizes what is actually a movement of meaning. When Jung in his late work said that the psyche thinks, Giegerich takes the sentence with Hegelian seriousness. The phenomenon, the symptom, the dream, wants to be thought through to its notion. Psychology’s task is to follow that self-movement, dialectically, until the image has been interiorized into the concept it was already trying to be. A psychology that stops at the image, and encourages the patient to live with the figure, has, on his account, refused the soul’s own next act.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Moore writes, from a background in a religious order and from a long reading of Hillman and of Marsilio Ficino, against a therapeutic culture whose aim is to cure the soul of its symptoms. Care, in the Renaissance sense he recovers from Ficino, is a tending, not a fixing. Depression, obsession, and the ordinary disorders of a household are the soul’s speech, and the work is to give them a worthy form rather than to silence them. The places of the work are ordinary: home, marriage, illness, a meal, a habit of beauty in daily things. He refuses both the clinic’s will to restore a functioning self and the fantasy that only a monastery is spiritual. Soul is the depth dimension of the life one is already in. The symptom is often the place where that dimension has been refused and is insisting.

He would rather educate the symptom than starve the ego. Set beside Pieper’s leisure, which this file cannot quote, the kinship is the defense of uselessness. A life scheduled entirely for function has already decided against the soul. Care is the reintroduction of times and objects that do not pay.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Iron John reads a Grimm tale as a sequence of initiation. A wild man is found at the bottom of a pool, brought into a castle, and becomes the secret teacher of a boy who has stolen a key and fled. Ashes, a wound, a garden, a war, and a return are stations. Bly’s claim, argued as a poet who had come to fairy tales through Jung and through the same interpretive tradition as von Franz, is that a culture without ritual descent produces men who either inflate or collapse. The wildness the tale hides under the water is not a permission to be violent. It is a vitality that has to be met, disciplined, and brought back. The wound is part of the education. A manhood that has never gone down is, in the book’s sense, still a boy in a king’s house, handling objects whose power he has not suffered.

The commentary is secondary, and at its worst it betrayed the tale. At its best it remembered that fairy stories are about the price of becoming a human being.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Corbin, the scholar of Suhrawardi and Ibn Arabi, argues for a world that our languages keep collapsing into two others. The imaginary is the unreal, the merely made-up. The intelligible is the abstract concept. Between them, in the Islamic Platonism he spent his life reading, lies the imaginal world, alam al-mithal, a real order of being perceived by an organ of imagination that can be trained. Allegory reduces it to a concept in fancy dress. The imaginal is his third term. quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Ta'wil, as Corbin explains it across his studies of Avicenna’s visionary recitals and of Ismaili hermeneutics, is a leading back. A text or an event is returned toward its origin, and the return is a spiritual act of the reader, who does not stand outside the text and translate it into a concept he already possessed. Allegory, in the sense he refuses, says: this image means that idea, and once the idea is had the image may be dropped. Ta'wil says: the image is the form in which a reality at another level of being becomes perceptible, and the reader’s own being is increased by perceiving it. Theophanic perception is the companion notion. What is truly seen is a face of the divine showing itself, not a sign pointing elsewhere. The seer and the seen are both implicated. A hermeneutic that leaves the reader unchanged has not performed ta'wil, whatever concepts it has extracted.

Corbin’s tradition multiplies them, because the only way the One shows itself to a finite perceiver is in a form. Williams’s two ways are the Christian statement of the same tension. quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Girard’s first claim is that desire is mimetic. We learn what to want from a model, and the model becomes a rival as soon as the wanting converges on an object that cannot be shared. The great novels, in Deceit, Desire and the Novel, are the texts that tell this truth against the romantic lie that desire is original, spontaneous, and one’s own. Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust, and Dostoevsky are his witnesses. The second claim, in Violence and the Sacred and The Scapegoat, is that a community in crisis discharges the rivalry onto a victim. The expulsion or the killing restores peace, and the peace is then told as a sacred story in which the victim is guilty and, often, later divine. Myth, on this reading, is the persecutor’s account. Biblical narrative, and the Gospels in particular, take the side of the victim and so begin to make the mechanism visible. He came to regard this unveiling as the reason for his own conversion to Christianity.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Gnostic Religion describes a syndrome. In the texts of late antique gnosis, the world is a prison made by lesser powers, the true self is a spark from beyond, and salvation is the remembering of an alien origin. Jonas argues that this is a dualism hostile to the cosmos, and that modern nihilism, after the death of a meaningful cosmic order, repeats the syndrome without the myth: a self for whom the universe is indifferent, and a contempt for nature dressed as honesty. He had been Heidegger’s student, and he came to think that existentialism shared the gnostic refusal of the world. The Imperative of Responsibility is the late mutation of the diagnosis. Technological action now reaches far beyond the actor’s lifetime and beyond the actor’s power to undo. Ethics has to answer for the future of vulnerable life. Nature is no longer the stage on which a self seeks its authenticity. It is the object of a duty, and the duty runs to generations who cannot consent.

God is the infinite actuality in which any finite thing exists at all: being, consciousness, and bliss as the names of that actuality, not as three qualities added to a large invisible person. quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Beauty, as Scruton defends it, is a reason. A face, a building, a melody, a stretch of country addresses a person and asks to be contemplated for its own sake. The experience is not a private pleasure one happens to have, and it is not a political instrument. It carries a summons: attend, and in attending become answerable to the thing. Much of what a century of criticism has said against beauty, that it is bourgeois, that it is a mask of power, that it is mere preference, he treats as a refusal of that summons. The Soul of the World extends the claim into a metaphysics of the sacred. Persons, home, and the edge of death disclose a world that looks back. The scientific image of objects in a causal field is real and incomplete. The world has a soul in the sense that it can be addressed and can address, and a culture that has lost the second-person relation to reality has lost the sacred even if it has kept the explanations.
