quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Unsettling of America describes a mind, the industrial mind, that treats land and body as raw material and calls the treatment progress. Against it Berry sets membership. A household, a farm, a small town, when they are working, are a single pattern of work, eating, care of the dead, and knowledge of a particular place. Fidelity to that place is an epistemology. One knows by staying, by suffering the consequences of one’s methods in the same soil one will hand on. Abstraction, the knowledge that can be applied anywhere because it is responsible nowhere, is the intellectual form of the unsettlement. He writes as a farmer and as a Christian, and the essays return to the same joint: a culture’s health is visible in how it eats, how it works, and whether its language can still tell the truth about both.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Pilgrim at Tinker Creek is a book of seeing, written from a year beside a creek in Virginia. Dillard distinguishes a kind of looking that searches, active and directed, from a kind of waiting in which something is given to a gaze that has stopped hunting. Both are disciplines. What they find is extravagant and violent as well as beautiful. The creek’s abundance, the insects, the waste, the particular cruelty of the natural world, are not edited into a lesson about harmony. Glory and cost arrive together, and the moral pressure of the book is to stay with what is actually there long enough that wonder becomes a perception rather than a mood one brought to the water. Seeing is compared, at times, to a stalking. It is also compared to a letting-go. The prose is the record of a person training both.

Cassirer’s philosophy of symbolic forms holds that myth, language, art, and science are not attempts, some failed and one successful, to copy a world that is already there. Each is a way of building a world. Man, in the formula of An Essay on Man, is the animal symbolicum. Myth is not bad science and not a childish science. It has its own principle of formation, its own way of configuring space, time, number, and the self. The task of a philosophy of culture is to understand these forms from the inside, as achievements of spirit, and to see how they generate the objects they then seem to find. The three volumes of The Philosophy of Symbolic Forms work the claim out for language, for mythical thought, and for the phenomenology of knowledge. The late Essay on Man is the shorter map.

Sind wir vielleicht hier, um zu sagen: Haus,
Brücke, Brunnen, Tor, Krug, Obstbaum, Fenster, –
höchstens: Säule, Turm… aber zu sagen, verstehs,
o zu sagen so, wie selber die Dinge niemals
innig meinten zu sein. Ist nicht die heimliche List
dieser verschwiegenen Erde, wenn sie die Liebenden drängt,
daß sich in ihrem Gefühl jedes und jedes entzückt?
Schwelle: was ists für zwei
Liebende, daß sie die eigne ältere Schwelle der Tür
ein wenig verbrauchen, auch sie, nach den vielen vorher
und vor den künftigen…, leicht.
Hier ist des Säglichen Zeit, hier seine Heimat.
Sprich und bekenn. Mehr als je
fallen die Dinge dahin, die erlebbaren, denn,
was sie verdrängend ersetzt, ist ein Tun ohne Bild.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
work: Duineser Elegien, „Die neunte Elegie“, Leipzig: Insel-Verlag, 1923, S. 34
expansion: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Duino Elegies ask what a human being is for, in a world where the animal seems at home and the angel seems terrible and remote. The Ninth Elegy turns the answer toward the earth. Things, the poem’s argument goes, want to be said. Saying is a transformation, not a description. What is visible is taken up into an inwardness and, in that sense, survives. The poet’s work is this work of transformation, and it is urgent because the earth needs it from us. The elegies do not hand the task to a church. They spend a Romantic inheritance, night and angel and a high unattainable beloved, on the praise of the perishable. Letters to a Young Poet, published in German in 1929 from letters written decades earlier, gives the accompanying ethic of a vocation: solitude, patience, the refusal to live by other people’s questions, and the counsel to live the questions themselves until one lives into an answer.

Novalis’s night is the ancestor the elegies both continue and spend differently. The hymn gives the night a sovereignty over the busy day. Rilke keeps a darkness and an angel and aims them at the saying of earthly things. The mutation is from a metaphysical night to an aesthetic of transience. Hölderlin’s sense of the poet’s task in a needy time is the other German ancestor, and Heidegger’s 1946 lecture on Rilke, ‘What Are Poets For?’, is the philosophical mutation of the elegies into a history of Being in a destitute age. That lecture should be read as Heidegger’s use of Rilke, not as Rilke’s own metaphysics. The poems remain poems of praise and of the difficulty of praise.

The Letters are the prose ethic that a century of readers has used as a manual of artistic seriousness. Their danger is the danger of any manual. Solitude and the lived question can become a style of postponement. Read beside the Ninth Elegy, they are stricter. The solitude is for the sake of a work that the earth, in the poem’s fiction, is waiting for. Goethe’s demand that the senses are how nature speaks, and Bachelard’s reverie on things, are the gentler cousins of this urgency. Rilke’s version hurts more, because the things are perishing and the saying is the only shelter he is willing to claim for them.

Copyright covers the English translations, so the poems are not quoted here. The German of 1923 and 1929 is the text. What can be said in prose is the claim the Ninth Elegy makes on a reader who loves things, landscapes, and works of art. Praise is a form of knowledge. It changes the one who praises and, in the poem’s sense, changes the status of the thing. A culture that only uses, catalogs, and displays has refused the transformation. The elegies are the demand that it be accepted.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Four Quartets takes the problem of time that ‘Tradition and the Individual Talent’ had stated as a critical doctrine and tries to live it. A moment in a rose garden, a wartime watch, a chapel at Little Gidding, each becomes a place where a life is answerable to more than succession. The poems refuse two escapes. One is the flight out of time into a timeless absolute that cancels history. The other is the reduction of meaning to historical process, as if the present were only the latest fact. What they circle is a stillness that is inside movement, and an Incarnation, in the Christian sense Eliot had accepted in 1927, as the place where the timeless and the temporal meet. The later quartets correct the early essay’s coldness about personality. Impersonality returns as humility, and as the acceptance of a life that cannot be made significant by the will alone. Dante, the Bhagavad Gita, and the English contemplative tradition, John of the Cross echoed rather than explained, are inside the sequence. Little Gidding the place is Nicholas Ferrar’s community, a historical prayer inside a poem about history.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Florensky, a priest, mathematician, and engineer who was executed in 1937, wrote The Pillar and Ground of the Truth as a series of letters to a friend. Truth, in the book’s central argument, is antinomic. The law of identity, the A that is only A, is the form of a dead self-sameness. A living truth holds contradictories together without collapsing into nonsense, and the Trinity is the pattern of that holding: identity that is also relation. Love is not an illustration of the pattern. Love, and friendship in particular, is the way the pattern is known. A truth that cannot be entered by a personal bond is, for him, a truth of objects. The letters are also a refusal of the split between exact thought and holy thought. A man who worked on electricity and on icons did not regard the combination as a hobby beside a profession. The antinomy is in the things, and a thinking that has forbidden antinomy has forbidden the things.

It is the long project, from the industrial revolution through the present systems of computation and control, by which a living world is converted into resource, process, and standing reserve, and by which human beings are reshaped to match. Progress is the project’s moral language. Against the Machine, published in 2025 as the gathering of three decades of this argument, treats the project as a spiritual form. What it hollows out is attention, place, memory, and the capacity to regard anything as sacred. The essays that led to the book, many of them written in public as the Abbey of Misrule, track the same claim through culture and through his own movement from ecological despair toward Christianity. The remedy he points at is not a better device. It is a recovery of roots in place, in work, and in a discipline of the spirit that can tell the Machine no.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Shop Class as Soulcraft argues that skilled manual work is a form of knowledge and a form of character, because the material pushes back. A motorcycle, a board, a pipe, will not ratify a careless idea. The worker learns a submission to a reality that is not his intention, and the submission is the education. The cultural prestige of mental work, and the tracking of whole populations away from the trades, is for Crawford a loss of that education and a loss of the kind of agency that comes from being able to see a situation and act in it competently. The World Beyond Your Head extends the claim to attention. A self is not a set of preferences. A self is made of what it can attend to, and a culture that engineers attention in order to capture it dissolves the person into a series of stimuli. Individuality, truly understood, is a situated competence. It is not the freedom to choose among options someone else has designed.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Vervaeke, a cognitive scientist at the University of Toronto, argues that the culture’s crisis is a crisis of meaning in a precise sense. It is not a shortage of information and not, primarily, a shortage of beliefs. It is a breakdown in the kinds of knowing by which a life becomes significant, and in the practices that train those kinds of knowing. He distinguishes propositional knowing, knowing that something is the case, from procedural knowing, knowing how, from perspectival knowing, knowing what it is like from here, and from participatory knowing, knowing what it is like to be in a relationship that shapes the knower. Relevance realization is the process, which he has also studied experimentally, by which an organism selects from an unmanageable world the things that matter for the action now required. The lecture series Awakening from the Meaning Crisis, fifty talks given in 2019, tells a history of how the traditional ecologies of this knowing, religion, initiation, craft, and contemplation, came apart, while propositional knowledge scaled. Zombies in Western Culture, written with Christopher Mastropietro, treats the figure of the zombie as a myth of a life that moves without meaning.

The series is a contemporary attempt to put Plotinus, the contemplative traditions, Zen, and a cognitive account of attention in one argument. Corbin’s imaginal is discussed as a mode of participatory knowing that a purely propositional culture cannot see. Jung and the symbolic life appear as modern attempts to recover what the ecology once trained. Vervaeke is not a disciple of these sources. A contemplative claim is asked to show up as a claim about how minds actually work.

The kinship with Taylor is the diagnosis of a malaise inside a secular frame. Taylor’s is historical and moral. Vervaeke’s is cognitive and practical. Crawford’s enclosure of attention is the economic side of the same corruption. Gebser’s deficient mental is what a mind looks like when only the propositional level is allowed to count as knowledge.

The series is public, and the books are his wording. This paraphrase is a map of the thesis.
